assertions.text: The response states that a planning horizon ending at age 85 is too short for a couple.
assertions.evidence: audit.md §9 "The horizon stops at 85": "For a couple currently 60 and 58, planning to Alex's 85 is planning to roughly a coin flip. The chance that at least one of you is alive at 90 is substantial... I've run everything to Alex 95 (2061). That is the number that matters."

assertions.text: The response identifies that applying the same average return every year hides the risk that poor returns early in drawdown produce far worse outcomes than the average implies.
assertions.evidence: §8 "An average return is not a return sequence": "bad years early sell more units to fund the same spending, and there's less left to recover" — "Three years at −6%... runs dry at Alex 94" vs reversed "ends with £886,132. Identical average... A single-average spreadsheet cannot see this."

assertions.text: The response identifies that the £42,000 annual spending is never increased for inflation anywhere in the model.
assertions.evidence: "The 6.5% is a **nominal** return... But spending sits at £42,000 in every row, and the state pension at £10,600 in every row. So the sheet grows the assets with inflation and holds the costs without it. £42,000 in 2051 buys what **£22,654** buys today." (§1 "Inflation is missing")

assertions.text: The response states that the State Pension start age of 66 used in the model is incorrect or unverified for at least one of the two partners.
assertions.evidence: "**Both state pension ages are a year early.** Yours is **67, not 66**" and audit.md §3 "Both state pension ages are a year too early... Alex (born May 1966): reaches 67 in **May 2033**, not 2032. Sam (born September 1968): reaches 67 in **September 2035**, not 2034."

assertions.text: The response flags the £203.85 weekly State Pension figure as out of date or as needing a current-year source.
assertions.evidence: "**The £203.85/week is the 2023/24 rate.** 2026/27 is £241.30/week = £12,548" (response), and audit.md §4: "The state pension figure is stale... £203.85/week was the **2023/24** rate", plus a GOV.UK 2026/27 rates source link.

assertions.text: The response identifies that treating withdrawals as gross-of-tax overstates what the pots deliver, because pension drawdown beyond the tax-free portion is taxed as income.
assertions.evidence: audit.md §5: "Your note says 'gross-of-tax — keeps it simple.' ... 25% of each pension withdrawal is tax-free ... Every pound of pension drawdown after that is taxed." Quantified: "about £3,660/year, roughly £92,000 over the plan ... a 9% increase on the withdrawal you need and the sheet has it at zero," plus £953,343→£882,796 in the tax correction row.

assertions.text: The response identifies that the order or mix of withdrawals across the pensions, ISAs, and cash changes the tax owed.
assertions.evidence: audit.md §5: "each of you can draw £16,760/year and pay nothing (£12,570 of it taxable, exactly filling your personal allowance)... Two of you gives £33,520 tax-free, and the ISA covers the remaining £8,480." Model code: "ISA / cash next (tax-free, preserves pension tax shelter)"; "split to stay in basic rate".

assertions.text: The response states that the planner's 100% success rate depends on its automatic spending cuts, so it does not demonstrate that £42,000 of spending is sustainable.
assertions.evidence: "'100% success' means you never ran out, given you accepted living on £31,500 whenever markets went badly. It's not testing the plan in your spreadsheet." Also audit.md: "A definition of success that includes a £10,500 pay cut will report success very reliably."

assertions.text: The response states what annual spending could fall to in the planner's poor scenarios, or identifies that the planner summary omits how low spending goes and for how long.
assertions.evidence: "Dynamic Spending™ cuts spending by up to 25% in poor markets — **that's £31,500**." And in audit.md: "A 25% cut to £42,000 is **£31,500**. So '100% success' means... you accepted living on as little as £31,500 whenever markets went badly."

assertions.text: The response gives an explicit overall answer on whether the couple can afford to retire this year.
assertions.evidence: "**Can you retire this year on £42,000?** Probably yes, but not with the margin the sheet implies." and audit.md's "Bottom line: You can probably retire this year, but not on £42,000... £38,000–£39,000 is the figure that buys a comfortable margin."

assertions.text: The response states a corrected figure for at least one identified error, such as what annual spending becomes in later years once inflated, or the gross withdrawal needed to net £42,000 after tax.
assertions.evidence: "£42,000 in 2051 buys what **£22,654** buys today, and £2,217,961 in 2051 is **£1,196,347** in today's money" — plus the corrected pension rate "2026/27 is £241.30/week = £12,548 — £1,947/year more each" and the correction table ending at £595,437.
